messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
Let $M$ be a metric space. We prove that $(M, d)$ is complete if and only if every nested sequence of nonempty closed sets with vanishing diameter has a nonempty intersection.

First assume $M$ is complete. Let $(F_n)$ be a sequence of nonempty closed subsets such that $F_{n+1} \subset F_n$ and $\text{diam}(F_n) \to 0$. Since each $F_n$ is nonempty, we can select an element $x_n \in F_n$ for each $n$. Consider the sequence $(x_n)$. For any $m, n \ge N$, both $x_m$ and $x_n$ belong to $F_N$ because of the nesting property. Therefore, $d(x_m, x_n) \le \text{diam}(F_N)$. As $N \to \infty$, $\text{diam}(F_N) \to 0$, which implies that $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence. Because $M$ is complete, there exists a point $x \in M$ such that $x_n \to x$.

We now verify that this limit point belongs to all sets in the sequence. Fix an arbitrary index $k$. The tail of the sequence $(x_n)_{n \ge k}$ lies entirely within $F_k$. Since $F_k$ is closed and contains the convergent subsequence, it must contain the limit $x$. Thus, $x \in F_k$ for all $k$, meaning $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty F_n$ is nonempty. This direction establishes one side of the equivalence.

Now suppose that any sequence of nonempty closed subsets with the stated properties has a nonempty intersection. We must show that $M$ is complete. Let $(y_n)$ be an arbitrary Cauchy sequence in $M$. Define the set $F_n = \overline{\{y_k : k \ge n\}}$, which is the closure of the tail of the sequence starting at $n$. Each $F_n$ is closed by definition. Furthermore, $F_{n+1} \subset F_n$ because the tail starting at $n+1$ is a subset of the tail starting at $n$.

We calculate the diameter of these sets to check the second condition. Since $(y_k)_{k \ge n}$ is eventually close together due to being Cauchy, the distance between any two points in the tail is small. Specifically, for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $N$ such that $d(y_i, y_j) < \epsilon$ for all $i, j \ge N$. Consequently, $\text{diam}(F_n) \le \epsilon$ for all $n \ge N$. This proves that $\text{diam}(F_n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. By our hypothesis, the intersection $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty F_n$ contains some point $y$.

This point $y$ serves as the limit of the original sequence. To see this, note that $y \in F_n$ for all $n$, so $y$ is in the closure of $\{y_k : k \ge n\}$. This implies that for any $\delta > 0$, there are infinitely many indices $k$ such that $d(y, y_k) < \delta$. More directly, since $y \in \overline{\{y_k : k \ge n\}}$ for all $n$, the distance $d(y, y_k)$ must go to zero as $k \to \infty$. Thus, $y_n \to y$, proving that every Cauchy sequence converges in $M$. Therefore, $M$ is complete.
